title: It is inconceivable to think Russia did not try to interfere in Brexit vote, says PM
description: Andy Burnham has said it is "inconceivable" to think that Russia did not try to interfere in the 2016 EU referendum.The prime minister told MPs he had
body: Andy Burnham has said it is "inconceivable" to think that Russia did not try to interfere in the 2016 EU referendum.The prime minister told MPs he had not been questioning the legitimacy of the Brexit vote, when he told the Rest is Politics podcast that it was "clear" there had been interference by Moscow.His comments to the podcast provoked angry responses from some Brexit campaigners with Reform UK leader Nigel Farage, calling the prime minister "a liar".A No 10 spokesperson said that while the prime minister believed it was highly likely Russia tried to influence the referendum result, he did not believe those efforts were successful.In an interview, released on Monday, Burnham told The Rest is Politics podcast,, external that upon arriving in Downing Street, he had asked if there had been Russian interference in the vote, adding: "I've had the clear answer that, yes, there was."He added: "I think we've been too much on the back foot on that actually and we haven't informed people sufficiently about the extent to which people are seeking to disrupt the political process from overseas."Burnham did not provide details about the extent or nature of Russian activities in the referendum during the interview and when pressed on the subject in the House of Commons on Monday afternoon appeared to be less definitive.Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch said the prime minister had "implied that the referendum result was illegitimate because of Russian interference".She asked the prime minister to confirm that he believed the referendum was legitimate adding: "If not, will he publish the evidence that Russia swung the result of the 2016 referendum."Burnham said he had "implied no such thing" but added that it was a "matter of record" that Russia sought to interfere in the 2019 general election."We think it is inconceivable that this was the first time," he said. Lib Dem leader Sir Ed Davey welcomed Burnham's comments, saying it "took courage after the Conservatives took so long suppressing the evidence".He also urged the prime minister to publish evidence of interference in the Brexit referendum as well as other UK votes. Burnham did not commit to making public any evidence but said he wanted to ensure that the British democratic system was protected in the future. Responding to Burnham's initial comments earlier in the day, Farage said: "The prime minister is a liar, yes, a liar.""There was no Russian interference - the Russian hoax has run all the way through this," he added. "This is out-of-touch, out-of-date Andy Burnham with all sorts of bizarre ideas."Former prime minister Boris Johnson wrote on X that in 2016, when he became foreign secretary the security services had told him "there was no evidence of any successful interference in the 2016 referendum, by Russia or any other power".He added: "Either the security services have changed their view - which would be very odd - or Burnham is lying about what he has been told."In 2020, a parliamentary report did not reach a firm conclusion on whether Russia had tried to intervene in UK elections and referendums, but criticised the government for failing to fully assess and counter the threat from Russian 'troll' accounts on social media.Asked in 2017, if he had seen evidence of Russia successfully meddling in UK elections, Johnson, who was then-foreign secretary said: "Nyet [Russian for no], not a sausage."Earlier this year, the government published an independent review, external on foreign influence in UK politics which said there were attempts to "sow distrust and exacerbate divisions in UK society with the ultimate aim of undermining confidence in our democracy". Report author Philip Rycroft said it was difficult to establish the impact of these efforts and that the public "can be credited with sufficient common sense to see of the more egregious attempts to suborn their opinions". However, he added that while there was no "immediate crisis" in British democracy "there is no guarantee that this will persist".

schema.headline: It is inconceivable to think Russia did not try to interfere in Brexit vote, says PM

title: Immigration agents search Congresswoman Ilhan Omar's home
description: "For ten years, Trump has targeted me with baseless lies and smear campaigns," Omar said in a statement. "This is just the latest escalation in his ca
body: "For ten years, Trump has targeted me with baseless lies and smear campaigns," Omar said in a statement. "This is just the latest escalation in his campaign of political intimidation. I will not be silenced."Her communications director Jacklyn Rogers called the raid "an outrageous abuse of power" by the Trump administration. "The Congresswoman has done nothing wrong."The nature of the criminal investigation remains unclear. A BBC crew saw several agents at the home, some carrying boxes to a van. News of the search was first reported by Fox News, which has said the investigation is about immigration paperwork filed by her late father when Omar was a child.The timing of Monday's raid - 22 days before the November midterm elections which will decide the balance of power in Congress for the next two years - has raised concerns from Democrats who have rallied behind Omar.The justice department has a longstanding policy of refraining from most enforcement action that is "likely to raise an issue or the perception" it was being brought for the purpose of affecting any election or disadvantage a candidate.The US House Democratic Party leadership said in a statement that Omar had long been targeted with "vile personal attacks and baseless accusations" by Trump. "Now, less than 30 days until the midterm election, his violent mass deportation machine has descended upon the home of a duly elected Member of Congress and her family," it said.Omar's immigration records have been scrutinised in the past by Republicans. Earlier this year, fellow Congresswoman Nancy Mace of South Carolina unsuccessfully filed a subpoena of her records.Last month, Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin told a conservative podcaster "something is going to happen", making allegations of marital fraud against Omar. Separately, the White House border tsar Tom Homan told Fox News that Omar was being investigated for unspecified immigration violations.Omar denied these allegations last month. "I will say it again so it's as clear as possible: I'm not at all worried about these investigations, because they are complete shams," she said in a campaign fundraising email, an archive of which has been seen by the BBC. She has been targeted by Trump with the president previously suggesting that she "should go back" to Somalia and that she should be deported. US citizenship is required to serve as a US House Representative.Omar has responded to Trump's insults and attacks describing them as an "unhealthy and creepy obsession".The president has also spoken unfavourably about the Somali American community. Last week, he wrote on social media that Minnesota "is being taken over by Somali immigrants" and said "the people of Minnesota must fight back."Some Republicans celebrated the search. "Nobody is above the law," said Minnesota Representative Tom Emmer. "We look forward to learning more details about this raid and investigation. ACCOUNTABILITY IS COMING!"Omar is the first Somali-American elected to the US House of Representatives and she represents a district in the Minneapolis area. She and Michigan Representative Rashida Tlaib were the first Muslim women elected to Congress.She won the 2024 election with 74% of the vote. Senior political leaders in Minnesota have also criticised the search. Governor Tim Walz criticised the search on Monday. "Americans see this for what it is - President Trump is abusing his power to go after political opponents weeks before an election."Minnesota senator Tina Smith called it "a transparent attempt to interfere in our elections."Additional reporting by Ione Wells

schema.headline: Immigration agents search Congresswoman Ilhan Omar's home

title: Miliband says Britain won't tolerate threats on our soil, as Iran ambassador summoned
description: The foreign secretary has summoned the Iranian ambassador to make clear that "Britain will not tolerate threats on our soil" following last month's in
body: The foreign secretary has summoned the Iranian ambassador to make clear that "Britain will not tolerate threats on our soil" following last month's incident at RAF Fairford.Ed Miliband said attempts by Iran to undermine the UK's security "through its criminal networks, proxy groups and state-backed malign activity is unacceptable".Prime Minister Andy Burnham told MPs the incident in Gloucestershire was "almost certainly directed by Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard", while the home secretary said the likely coordinator was a "known individual based in Iran".Iran's ambassador to the UK, Seyed Ali Mousavi, said Tehran was not involved and was willing to cooperate with British authorities.The Foreign Office has also sanctioned two Iranians, including the head of the regime's counterespionage operations - with both men subjected to travel bans and asset freezes.Burnham also indicated Iran could be hit with further sanctions over its suspected role.It comes as the UK and 28 other countries - including the US, Canada, Australia, France and Germany - issued a joint statement condemning "in the strongest terms" violent attacks by Iran. The statement accuses Tehran of carrying out "lethal plotting, arson, sabotage, cyber-attacks, and other hybrid activities" and also recognises the UK's attribution of Iranian involvement in the incident at RAF Fairford.A huge police operation began after officers were alerted to three suspicious vehicles near the base in the early hours of 27 September.Dozens of homes were evacuated in the nearby village of Whelford and a large cordon was put in place around the site.So far, a total of seven men - all in their 20s - have been arrested and later bailed in connection with the incident. No one has been charged.Last week, Downing Street insisted the airbase was safe after the US withdrew all of its bombers – about a dozen B-1s from the base – back to their home stations on American soil.In July, Iran said "any base used for aggression against Iranian territory constitutes a legitimate target for our forces".RAF Fairford, in the Cotswolds, has been used as a forward operating location by the US air force for decades.In recent months, the US has flown B-1 and B-52 bombers from the base for the Middle East, after the UK approved an American request to use it for defensive strikes on Iran.A US state department spokesman confirmed that US Secretary of State Marco Rubio had a call with Miliband on Monday where they discussed "holding Iran to account for its actions and of continued collaboration to secure US assets in the United Kingdom".

schema.headline: Miliband says Britain won't tolerate threats on our soil, as Iran ambassador summoned

title: Tom Cruise film Digger forecast to lose $245m as The Social Recknoning also struggles at box office
description: Tom Cruise's latest film Digger is expected to lose around $245m (£185m), Hollywood analysts have said, after the film's continuing poor performance a
body: Tom Cruise's latest film Digger is expected to lose around $245m (£185m), Hollywood analysts have said, after the film's continuing poor performance at the box office.Ticket sales for the satirical black comedy, which stars Cruise as oil magnate Digger Rockwell, dropped by around 60% in the movie's second weekend in cinemas.It brings Digger's total box office takings so far to around $35m (£26m) globally. The film is estimated to have cost its studio Warner Bros around $280m (£211m) to make and market.But Cruise said last week, external that he "never thought of movies when I'm making them [in terms of] opening weekend," adding he was instead focused on making films that "hopefully will translate, last and evolve".The film's box office takings relative to its budget mean it could become one of the biggest film flops in Hollywood history.That would put Digger in the same bracket as other films which lost upwards of $100m, including 1995's Cutthroat Island, 2002's The Adventures of Pluto Nash, 2005's Sahara and 2012's John Carter. Other films estimated to have lost nine-figure sums include Mars Needs Moms (2011), Amsterdam (2022), The 13th Warrior (1999), The Marvels (2023) and Speed Racer (2008).Digger's performance stands in sharp contrast to the success of major franchises starring Cruise in recent years, such as new instalments of Top Gun and Mission: Impossible.Hollywood trade publication Variety said Digger was expected to end its box office run with around $50m (£38m) worldwide.The film would need around $350m (£264m) to break even, due to its budget, marketing costs, the portion of ticket sales that go to theatres and the likely spend on an awards season campaign.However, a Warner Bros spokesman pushed back slightly on the figure, telling Variety the film's break even point was $300m (£227m).Digger was the last standalone release for the studio before its recent takeover by Paramount.The film is directed by Alejandro G Iñárritu, best known for films such as Birdman, Babel and The Revenant.Digger received generally poor reviews from critics, prompting Warner Bros to launch a new marketing campaign urging audiences to "decide for yourself". Meanwhile, the new sequel to the Oscar-winning hit The Social Network also struggled at the box office on its opening weekend.The Social Reckoning took $5.5m (£4.1m) in the US, significantly lower than the $22m (£16m) its predecessor took on its opening weekend in 2010, not adjusted for inflation.Globally, Aaron Sorkin's latest film, starring Mikey Madison, Jeremy Strong and Jeremy Allen White, took around $9m (£6.8m).The film tells the true story of a Facebook engineer, Frances Haugan, who leaked internal documents to a reporter after becoming concerned about some of the company's practices.The Social Reckoning was beaten in the US box office chart by horror movie Other Mommy, psychological thriller Verity, video game adaptation Resident Evil and Brad Pitt's wilderness thriller Heart of the Beast.

schema.headline: Tom Cruise film Digger forecast to lose $245m as The Social Recknoning also struggles at box office

title: Why Moscow is staying tight-lipped on Trump's energy ceasefire
description: On Sunday, US President Donald Trump announced that Russia and Ukraine had agreed a ceasefire on strikes on energy infrastructure "effective immediate
body: On Sunday, US President Donald Trump announced that Russia and Ukraine had agreed a ceasefire on strikes on energy infrastructure "effective immediately". Ukraine's Volodymyr Zelensky suggested it was "news for me", while Russia has not commented publicly.So who is saying what?Donald Trump says an energy ceasefire has been agreed.Kyiv asks: Has it? It is willing to sign up – if Russia does.Russia is saying: Very little.Russian President Vladimir Putin's spokesman Dmitry Peskov was asked whether such a ceasefire had been agreed during his daily conference call with journalists."Contacts are continuing," Peskov replied. "As soon as we have anything to say about this, we will definitely inform you."Peskov may not have had much to say on the matter, but the pro-Kremlin media has.It has dubbed President Trump's announcement of an energy ceasefire "a gift" for Moscow."Of course we benefit," pro-government news outlet Moskovsky Komsomolets concluded."It means that all Russia has to do is not destroy Ukraine's last remaining oil refinery. "That has already been attacked several times. It's barely functioning anyway."But Kyiv won't be allowed to hit the multitude of refineries we have. "In effect it's a one-way deal that benefits us. That's why no one here has officially rejected it."In other words, Moscow believes Trump's announcement ties Ukraine's hands, not Russia's.In recent months, long-range Ukrainian drone strikes on Russian oil facilities have caused extensive damage, as well as fuel shortages across the country. Should such attacks continue, expect the Russians to claim that Kyiv is harming US economic interests – as well as the Republican Party's chances in the midterm elections in November.Russian officials will argue that the strikes undermine the recent Trump-Putin fuel deal for the US to import Russian diesel. Trump has claimed the agreement will benefit US consumers, although there is widespread scepticism that the volumes involved will do much to lower fuel prices.Still, the Kremlin will be only too happy if Ukrainian drone strikes on oil facilities spark fury in the White House and curtail US support for Kyiv. Moscow would welcome Washington cutting off intelligence sharing to Ukraine and weapons sales to Europe that are destined for Kyiv.It has already delighted to hear Trump declaring: "I think it's time for Ukraine to get a new president."Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky has called for a 60-day Russian ceasefire to allow for presidential elections in Ukraine.Moscow's reaction?"The Kremlin, the president, has said many times before, we don't want a ceasefire, we want a lasting peace, and we're willing to do whatever's possible for that," Peskov said."Whatever's possible" does not include a 60-day ceasefire, or a 30-day ceasefire, or anything close to that.On Monday, the Kremlin proposed a one-day cessation of hostilities for Ukraine to hold elections.That will not be seen in Ukraine, or in the West, as a serious offer.It comes as no surprise though.Putin has shown little desire to halt the fighting. Recent statements, speeches and signals from Russia's leader suggest that, with winter approaching, the Kremlin is counting on a continued campaign of Russian strikes to significantly increase the pressure on Ukraine.On Monday, Russia's Foreign Minister Sergei Lavrov said Ukraine does not deserve the "respite" a ceasefire would bring.The Kremlin has claimed to seek "lasting peace" but right now it is continuing the fighting.On Monday, Zelensky claimed that Russia had hit several energy targets across Ukraine during the night and into the morning."This window of opportunity should be used to knock Ukraine back to the Stone Age and force it to accept peace on Russia's terms," the pro-government Moskovsky Komsomolets has written.The Kremlin's objective hasn't changed: Ukraine's capitulation.Moscow seems to believe that the diesel deal with Trump and the US president's growing impatience with Zelensky will help Russia secure its goal.

schema.headline: Why Moscow is staying tight-lipped on Trump's energy ceasefire

title: Six Ukrainian energy sites hit by Russia since Trump announced ceasefire, Zelensky says
description: Image source, EPAImage caption, Emergency services responded to a Russian drone strike on a residential building in Kharkiv, north-eastern Ukraine on
body: Image source, EPAImage caption, Emergency services responded to a Russian drone strike on a residential building in Kharkiv, north-eastern Ukraine on MondayByOlivia Ireland and Ella KiplingUpdated 3 hours agoRussia struck six Ukrainian energy facilities hours after US President Donald Trump announced the two countries had agreed to an energy ceasefire, Volodymyr Zelensky has said.Despite Trump stating on Sunday the truce would be "effective immediately", the Ukrainian president said Russia had hit "our gas stations, energy infrastructure, and other facilities".There were blackouts in the city of Izyum after a Russian strike destroyed power grids, Ukraine's state news agency Ukrinform said, while energy and railway infrastructure in western Ukraine was also targeted overnight.On Monday, Russia's Foreign Minister Sergei Lavrov said Ukraine does not deserve the "respite" a ceasefire would bring.Zelensky said 33 people had been injured in the strikes on energy facilities across the country.He told Fox News: "We did not attack, while Russia attacked our gas stations, energy infrastructure, and other facilities.""I think it was Putin's answer to President Trump," he added.Global conflicts have pushed fuel prices higher ahead of the US midterm elections and on Friday Trump announced a plan to import Russian diesel into the US on Friday.On Monday, Ukraine's state-owned grid operator Ukrenergo reported "new power cuts" in Kharkiv, Donetsk and Zaporizhzhia due to damage caused to energy equipment by Russian attacks.Electricity rationing has been introduced in parts of Ukraine to avoid overloading damaged equipment, Ukrenergo said.Zelensky said on X the strikes were proof Russia was "unwilling to accept an energy ceasefire".On Monday evening, Kyiv's mayor Vitali Klitschko posted on Telegram that a drone hit a 25-story residential building in the Darnytskyi district.Several cars in the building's courtyard were also on fire, he said, with one person dead and 11 injured.Figure caption, Watch: What could Trump's energy ceasefire claim mean for Ukraine?When Trump first announced the ceasefire on Sunday, Zelensky said it was "news to him" that a truce was in effect, but he backed the proposed ceasefire as a "major step toward ending the war, if the Americans truly step in now and make sure Russians respect the energy ceasefire".For months, Ukraine and Russia have been exchanging strikes on energy infrastructure, disrupting energy supplies on both sides.Moscow has said the installations it hits are legitimate targets as they support Ukraine's military operation, while Zelensky has characterised Ukrainian attacks deep inside Russian territory as part of an effort to "reduce Russia's ability to finance the war".Analysis by BBC Verify on both Ukrainian and Russian strikes during the war have found both sides have increased their attacks in the lead up to the next winter.In 2026, BBC Verify has recorded 273 strikes on Russian-controlled oil and gas facilities, more than double the 124 recorded over the same period in 2025.Separately, analysis of data aggregated by global conflict monitor, the Armed Conflict Location and Event Data project (Acled), recorded 2.4 times as many reported Russian attacks affecting Ukraine's energy network so far this year.Image source, EPA/ShutterstockImage caption, Energy facilities in Kharkiv were hit by Russian strikes on Sunday evening, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky saidTrump has been urging Ukraine to stop strikes on Russian oil infrastructure, so Russia can fulfil the recently struck deal to release diesel to the US and the global market.The deal temporarily undoes US sanctions on energy imports, which Zelensky described as a "gift" to Russian President Vladimir Putin.Figure caption, What's behind Trump's energy ceasefire claim?UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham said Britain "strongly supports President Trump's call today for a sustained energy ceasefire to start now", while France, Canada and the EU also expressed support.However, there has been a mixed response among European officials.EU foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas said the bloc would welcome an energy ceasefire "when it holds". Kallas said at a meeting of EU foreign ministers on Monday: "We haven't yet seen that also Russia will stick to it."Meanwhile, Estonia's foreign minister said the ceasefire was "not working".Additional reporting by Benedict Garman, BBC Verify

schema.headline: Six Ukrainian energy sites hit by Russia since Trump announced ceasefire, Zelensky says

title: South Africa vs Australia: Matt Renshaw stars again as tourists close on statement victory
description: First Test, Durban (day four of five)Australia 390 & 314-6 dec: Renshaw 82; Nortje 2-56, Maharaj 2-56South Africa 284 & 102-4: Bedingham 46, Markram 4
body: First Test, Durban (day four of five)Australia 390 & 314-6 dec: Renshaw 82; Nortje 2-56, Maharaj 2-56South Africa 284 & 102-4: Bedingham 46, Markram 45*; Hazlewood 2-20South Africa need 319 runs to win ScorecardAustralia are primed to earn a statement victory and end South Africa's unbeaten run under captain Temba Bavuma after Matt Renshaw's remarkable Test continued on day four of their series opener in Durban.Renshaw, in his second game back after a three-year absence, followed his 190 in the first innings with 89 to allow Australia to declare on 314-6. The 30-year-old then dismissed Bavuma with his part-time off-spin late in the day for his first Test wicket.Captain Pat Cummins followed with a perfect set-up of Tristan Stubbs - pushing him back with shorter balls before nicking him off with a full delivery - to leave South Africa 102-4 at the close.Set a world record 421 to win, they need to bat out the final day for a draw with six wickets remaining.South Africa have won 11 and drawn one of their Tests under Bavuma's captaincy, including their run to the 2025 World Test Championship final where they beat Australia at Lord's.This is the first Test in a South African summer that includes two more against the Australians, two against Bangladesh and three against England over Christmas.Even bad light, which cut short the first three days, did not come to South Africa's aid on the fourth evening. The Proteas' hopes rest largely on the shoulders of opener Aiden Markram who battled to 45 not out from 115 balls.The right-hander scored a sensational 136 against Australia in the fourth innings of their Test Championship final win and only one active player - Sri Lanka's Kusal Mendis - can better his average of 45.56 in the fourth innings of Tests.Dragging South Africa out of this position will require immense skill, however. Only twice has a team survived 140 overs to save a Test in the past 13 years.While Markram shared a stand of 66 in 19.4 overs with David Bedingham the pitch appeared becalmed, but by the close even Renshaw was finding extravagant turn.One thing in Markram's favour is he has now faced 313 balls from Australia's premier spinner Nathan Lyon in Tests and is yet to be dismissed.Australia may also be without the fielding excellence of Steve Smith. The former captain spent time off the field on day four having been hit on the helmet by a Anrich Nortje bouncer in making 27.After Ryan Rickelton top-edged a loose pull shot to Josh Hazlewood in the fourth over, Markram showed similar to restraint to that shown by Renshaw in his first-innings hundred.Renshaw again held Australia's innings together, but was more adventurous in his strokeplay to set up his side's declaration.Whether bad light returns on the final day may determine if the tourists were right to bat on until tea.

schema.headline: South Africa vs Australia: Matt Renshaw stars again as tourists close on statement victory

title: Fridges in French supermarkets hit by cyber attack
description: Hundreds of French supermarkets have been hit by a cyber attack that caused their fridges and freezers to heat up, spoiling fresh and frozen food esti
body: Hundreds of French supermarkets have been hit by a cyber attack that caused their fridges and freezers to heat up, spoiling fresh and frozen food estimated to be worth millions of euros.Hackers gained control of the software that regulates the temperatures of the refrigeration units, forcing some to warm to 50C (120F) overnight, according to one supermarket chain affected.The chief executive of Coopérative U said several of its supermarkets had been hit by the "extremely serious and unprecedented" attack. More than 100 of the chain's supermarkets were targeted, while 180 stores from Intermarché and its Netto brand were affected, with a spokesman saying that another 100 shops were urgently disconnected from the internet to prevent the same thing happening to them.Other major food retailers including Carrefour, Monoprix and E.Leclerc were also hit by the attack, which targeted software provided by Danish engineering firm Danfoss. The software allows retailers to manage their cold units remotely. Normally, supermarket freezers go through a short period of defrosting overnight, in which temperatures rise slightly. But the hackers ordered the units to heat up and stay hot, although Danfoss did not confirm any reports about just how warm the fridges and freezers could become in that process. Danfoss said the affected cold units were older models whose security software could not be updated to ward off a risk they had identified. The firm added in s statement that it had "long advised" businesses to keep supported systems up to date."Reliable refrigeration is critical to our customers' operations, and we remain committed to supporting our customers and helping them maintain secure and reliable systems they are used to."The full scale of the attack is unclear, but figures supplied by individual chains suggest about 400 stores were affected out of 15,000 or so overall in France. Carrefour said fridges in 80 of its 6,000 stores were hacked, while Monoprix said 5% of its 400-plus stores had been hit, with food removed from sale if its condition could not be guaranteed.In a statement to the BBC, Mousquetaires Group - which owns Intermarché and Netto - said some fresh and frozen food display units remained out of service on Monday afternoon. The stores had "taken all necessary precautions to remove the products from these units", it said, adding that staff were working to restock the shelves "as soon as possible".Intermarché said its fridges had heated up to 50C for six hours overnight into Monday, and the retailer had thrown away all the affected food to avoid health risks, the Reuters news agency reported.As a result of the attack, managers arriving at branches of several supermarket chains on Monday morning were hit by a wave of hot air from the freezers. In some places there were even small fires.French broadcaster BFMTV published an image showing a freezer in an ice cream aisle displaying a temperature of 26.5C.Two supermarkets in the Alsace region reported losses of €270,000 (£228,000) between them, the broadcaster added, meaning the nationwide total could run into the millions.French prosecutors have opened a specific cyber-crime investigation into the incident, which the Paris prosecutor's office called a "large-scale cyber-attack affecting the refrigerators of several major food retail chains across France". European Food Commissioner Christophe Hansen condemned the hack in a post on X and added: "Food security requires more attention at all levels. Because the weaponisation of food has become a reality."In a post on X, Coopérative chief executive Dominique Schelcher said staff were "fully mobilised, in co-ordination with refrigeration specialists, to restore the situation as quickly as possible".He called for an investigation into the hack and said targeting equipment essential to the French food supply was "unacceptable".Have you been affected by this cyber attack? Share your experience.

schema.headline: Fridges in French supermarkets hit by cyber attack

title: Unworn kit: What happens to it and why is there so much?
description: What happens to sports kit that never gets worn?Figure caption, What happens to unworn sports kit?ByBBC Sport correspondentFor an elite athlete, pulli
body: What happens to sports kit that never gets worn?Figure caption, What happens to unworn sports kit?ByBBC Sport correspondentFor an elite athlete, pulling on Olympic kit can be the reward for years of sacrifice. But some of that clothing never makes it out of the packaging.Inside a warehouse on England's south coast, boxes are stacked with pristine Team GB clothing from Paris 2024 and Milan Cortina 2026. Tracksuit bottoms, jackets, hoodies and T-shirts sit untouched. Among them are garments created for Olympic opening ceremonies. All of it is unworn.Commercial constraints can make excess stock difficult to shift at scale.Now a new partnership means hundreds of items of surplus Team GB clothing and unsold merchandise will be resold through a specialist platform, with proceeds supporting the British Olympic Association's (BOA) charity arm, the Team GB Foundation.The initial launch will include 700 items from Paris 2024.It is one way of giving sportswear a second life. But why does that surplus exist, and why can perfectly usable clothing be so difficult to pass on?Why does sport have so much spare kit?The BOA is far from the only organisation dealing with excess kit – elite sport in general struggles with kit wastage.5thread, a consultancy specialising in sustainability, estimates that up to 100,000 items of sports kit end up in UK landfill every year."It is a huge issue and it's also a complex issue," says Joanna Czutkowna, director of 5thread and a doctoral researcher in sports apparel and the circular economy."A lot of this kit is bought before they know which athletes are going to complete in the sport or the event. So there's a lot of excess stock generated at the point of order."Also, the types of contracts that you get for this have something called value in kind, so it's not a transactional contract. There's almost an incentive to get free product."Czutkowna is describing practices across elite sport, rather than Team GB's arrangements.Performance requirements also complicate efforts to reduce waste. Athletes need clothing designed to help them compete, so reducing quantities or changing materials is not always straightforward.The total surplus is difficult to measure. Kit can remain in warehouses or athletes' garages without entering a waste stream where it can be counted.The issue extends across sport, from clubs to countries.European football governing body Uefa estimates that up to 60% of professional team apparel, external is disposed of at the end of the season, although this figure has not been independently verified.Why not just give it away?The obstacles are not to do with the condition of the clothing."Contracts can prohibit reuse because they don't want it on the market or there might be a particular innovation that they want to hold back," Czutkowna says.Adam Stevens, co-founder of Kitround, the specialist resale platform working with Team GB among others, says sponsorship and supply agreements remain financially important to sport, but there are ways to respect them while allowing clothing to be used again."There are an awful lot of people, whatever sport they do, whatever teams they support, who simply can't afford to buy new," he says.Image source, Royal Yachting AssociationImage caption, British kitesurfer Lily Young training off the coast of Weymouth'Basically brand new' - but no longer the bestFor British kitesurfer Lily Young, who is targeting a place at the Los Angeles Olympics in 2028, the pressure to find a competitive edge can itself create surplus.Athletes preparing for major championships want to leave nothing to chance."That does mean that we also end up with a lot of waste - a lot of things where you're like, 'this is basically brand new, but it's not quite good enough to maybe win'."Changes in sponsors can also leave athletes with clothing they can no longer wear.Young and fellow athletes have passed T-shirts to younger squad members and youth teams. Wetsuits and other equipment can also be passed on where they remain suitable.But equipment that no longer meets an elite athlete's needs could help someone else start, and more organisations such as Sail GP and the Royal Yachting Association are using specialist platforms to sell second-hand elite kit to the public at much lower prices."We know that one of the main barriers to entry is cost," Young says.For Czutkowna, organisations need to think harder about how long their products can remain useful - and who could benefit from them."A lot of this comes back to common sense," she says. "It's kind of a waste not, want not."What is changing at Team GB?Jen Rouse, managing director of the Team GB Foundation, says ordering is becoming more precise and the amount left over is reducing.Team GB is also considering producing some clothing without dates or event-specific names, so it could be used across more than one Olympic cycle. It is also exploring opportunities for athletes to return clothing they no longer need.She rejects the suggestion that excess clothing has previously simply accumulated unused."It's not necessarily been sitting gathering dust in storage. It's always found a way out," she says.The partnership with Kitround creates another route, with sales supporting the Team GB Foundation.The aim is a circular economy for kit: keeping clothing and equipment in use through reuse, repair and resale.For Stevens, the principle behind finding kit another home is simple."A kit was made to be worn. It was made to be out there on the field, on the water, in the pool, and it should be back out there."That's really what underpins everything - making sure this kit doesn't go to landfill and that it can have a second life."

schema.headline: Unworn kit: What happens to it and why is there so much?

title: Women's World Cup qualifying: Do England lack ruthlessness in front of goal?
description: England's lack of ruthlessness in front of goal has been an occurring theme since 2023 when they finished runners-up to Spain in the World Cup.In that
body: England's lack of ruthlessness in front of goal has been an occurring theme since 2023 when they finished runners-up to Spain in the World Cup.In that tournament, they came through the group stage unconvincingly, beating lower-ranked opposition Haiti and Denmark, both 1-0.In the knockout stage, they got past Nigeria via a penalty shootout and had to come from behind to beat Colombia 2-1 in the quarter-finals.In World Cup qualifying this year, England have performed well but have not won with ease, edging past Iceland and Spain and under-firing against Greece.They are creating chances though, and had 58 touches in the opposition box against Greece and 210 passes in the final third."We played differently back then [in 2023]. There's a lot more pressure when you're at the World Cup," said midfielder Keira Walsh."In these [qualifying] games, the worrying thing would be if we were not arriving in the final third. That would be a bigger problem."It's the final pass, final cross and final shot. That was what was missing [on Friday]. I see the girls do that in training every day. They are fantastic at it. "It's just putting that in the game tomorrow and hopefully we will."Walsh said their hesitancy in front of goal was "frustrating" and they know there is work to do in the second leg.One player who has stepped up to the challenge is Arsenal midfielder Georgia Stanway, who is England's top scorer since Euro 2025 with 10 goals.She ranks inside the top three for most goals scored by European players in internationals and has a minutes-per-goal ratio of 81.Wiegman hopes others will follow suit and was clear on where she thinks the team can improve when asked about it on Monday."We got in good positions but then it's staying onside, having the final pass, the right pass at the right moment, the run at the right time and deciding what cross, what cutback and whether to go for the far post," added the Dutchwoman. "That is also about the connections between the players in those situations and taking out the counter-attack [threat]."England's problem is not a lack of talent but perhaps where best to utilise them.Chelsea's Lauren James has switched positions from being a winger, to a number 10 and even a centre-forward on occasion.Injuries to strikers Aggie Beever-Jones and Michelle Agyemang has meant there is little competition for Alessia Russo in the number nine role.Lauren Hemp has been in fantastic form but is not known for her goalscoring prowess, while Beth Mead is used in midfield as well as attack.Former England striker Ellen White, who remains the Lionesses all-time top scorer, believes building connections and setting the right tempo is crucial."You need to build your own rhythm. You can't just whizz the ball around quickly all the time so you need players in midfield who can dictate it," White told the Women's Football Weekly podcast. "You then have to have connections with players who are close to you, for example between a number 10 and a number nine. "Fran Kirby was like a dream for me because she could always put the ball near me and I felt like we had a good connection. You have to build those."The goals are at least being spread around the team with England having had 11 different goalscorers since Euro 2025.Defenders Lucy Bronze, Jess Carter and Maya le Tissier have all netted in the past 18 months, while England's number nine has added six to the tally. But England are still not clinical and have not won any games in which they have trailed since the end of Euro 2025, losing to Brazil and Spain on those occasions.Regular starter Hemp, who has played 687 minutes, has scored just twice, while the talented James has not found the back of the net in her past 425 minutes.Part of the problem has been that England have often come up against weaker opposition that sit in a low block and they have found it hard to break them down."The movement you have around the box is so important. You need to be unselfish in your movement," ex-England midfielder Kirby told Women's Football Weekly. "You need runs in behind, even if they won't get the ball. You have to entice teams to come out. You need one person to make a mistake and leave space. "You also need to pass to someone who has a higher percentage shot position than you. It seemed rushed [against Greece] instead of controlled. "You have to be intricate in and around the box."

title: Saudi minister vows 'serious response' to Houthi attacks on airports
description: Saudi Arabia's energy minister has vowed a "serious" response to the deadly attacks on the kingdom's airports and oil and gas facilities by Yemen's Ir
body: Saudi Arabia's energy minister has vowed a "serious" response to the deadly attacks on the kingdom's airports and oil and gas facilities by Yemen's Iran-backed Houthi movement."The events of recent weeks are serious. Our response must be equally serious," Prince Abdul Aziz bin Salman told the WPC Energy Congress in Riyadh.On Sunday, a Pakistani man was killed in an attack on a terminal at the capital's King Khalid International Airport, Saudi authorities said. It came a day after a Houthi missile hit another terminal, killing 13 people and forcing its closure.The Houthis said they launched the attacks in retaliation for "brutal Saudi aggression" against areas they control in western Yemen.The Houthi-run health ministry said a child was killed and six other people were injured in a Saudi air strike on a home in the capital, Sanaa, on Sunday.A Saudi-led coalition is providing air support for Yemeni pro-government forces battling the Houthis on Yemen's Red Sea coast and other areas.The WPC Energy Congress opened on Sunday at a convention centre about 10km (6 miles) from Riyadh's airport, which has been attacked four times over the past week.Last Thursday, three Saudis, including a pilot for the national airline Saudia, were killed in two strikes on an airport facility and an aircraft on the ground.Another four Saudis, as well as two Bangladeshis, one American, one Egyptian, one Jordanian, one Syrian, one Palestinian, one Sudanese and one Indian, were killed in Saturday's missile strike on Terminal 3.On Sunday, a Pakistani resident was killed when a projectile hit Terminal 4, according to the General Authority of Civil Aviation (GACA).King Fahd International Airport in the north-eastern city of Dammam was also attacked on Sunday evening, it said, but no casualties were reported.Later, the Saudi-led coalition said its forces had intercepted a drone in Eastern Province and a missile launched by the Houthis towards the south-western city of Khamis Mushait.In his inaugural address to the WPC Energy Congress on Monday, Prince Abdul Aziz thanked industry executives and policymakers for attending despite the attacks."You know this country is safe and that we hold your protection at whole heart," he said.But he also acknowledged that "energy security cannot be taken for granted" and that recent developments had "tested our infrastructure, our institutions, our people, and our resilience".Prince Abdul Aziz promised that his country would overcome those challenges."We, as Saudis, are fearless, combatant and determined people," he said. "We shall prove it to the world that whatever we are going through we will overcome it."There was no immediate comment from the Houthis.On Sunday evening, Houthi military spokesman Yahya Sarea said in a video statement that its forces had launched missiles and drones at Riyadh and Dammam's airports, as well as two oil and gas facilities in Eastern Province, in response to 124 Saudi air strikes in Yemen over the previous 24 hours.Sarea also reiterated a warning to airlines and passengers against using Saudi airports and airspace, except for journeys to and from the Islamic holy cities of Mecca and Medina.The Houthis' forces, he vowed, would "continue their escalating operations deep inside Saudi, imposing the equation of 'a blockade for a blockade' and 'an escalation for an escalation' and targeting Saudi enemy reinforcements until the aggression ceases and the siege on our dear people is lifted".Saturday's attack on Riyadh airport drew widespread international condemnation.UN Secretary General António Guterres said he was "deeply shocked" and warned that attacks on civilians and civilian infrastructure were a violation of international law.President Donald Trump said he would "make a decision" about the US joining Saudi Arabia's strikes on the Houthis. The US military is reportedly already providing intelligence and targeting support to the Saudi-led coalition.Iran, which has repeatedly denied allegations that it provides weapons and training to the Houthis, said it was "deeply concerned" by the escalation and called for "dialogue and engagement" to resolve the situation.Yemen has been devastated by a civil war that began in 2014, when the Houthis ousted the government from Sanaa. The conflict escalated in 2015, after the Saudi-led coalition intervened in an attempt to restore the government's rule.A four-year-old informal ceasefire began to unravel in July, when the Houthis announced a "maritime embargo" against Saudi Arabia and began missile and drone attacks on Saudi airports, oil facilities and tankers in the Red Sea.The Houthis said they were retaliating for what they call a Saudi blockade of ports and airports in their territory, as well as an air strike on Sanaa airport that they blamed on the kingdom. The Yemeni government claimed it was behind that strike, saying it was trying to prevent an unauthorised Iranian plane from landing.Last month, the Houthis launched a surprise offensive along Yemen's south-western Red Sea coast and ousted pro-government forces from areas overlooking the Bab al-Mandab Strait, at the southern end of the Red Sea.They said they posed no threat to international shipping passing through the waterway but that they would continue to target vessels from Saudi Arabia.However, the seizure of the strait contributed to a surge in global oil prices because Saudi Arabia had been relying on the Red Sea for oil exports after the US and Israel's war with Iran effectively closed the Strait of Hormuz in the Gulf.Last week, the Yemeni government announced the start of a new offensive aimed at retaking all territory held by the Houthis.Pro-government forces said they were quickly able to retake areas around Bab al-Mandab with the help of intense Saudi air strikes, but the Houthis denied losing any territory.

title: Afghanistan Premier League: Ollie Pope withdraws from draft
description: England batter Ollie Pope has pulled out of the draft for the Afghanistan Premier League.Pope had been due to be the only centrally contracted England
body: England batter Ollie Pope has pulled out of the draft for the Afghanistan Premier League.Pope had been due to be the only centrally contracted England player in the running for the inaugural edition of the APL, which is set to take place in the United Arab Emirates later this year.On Monday, when England's latest batch of contracts were confirmed, director of cricket Rob Key said he would not play in the APL but it is "legally hard" to prevent England players from taking part.In order for any English player to take part in the league they would require a No Objection Certificate from the England and Wales Cricket Board (ECB).With batter Pope being a contracted player, Key would have been involved in deciding the Surrey man's availability for the APL.However, it is understood Pope has taken the decision to withdraw from the draft taking place later this month independently of Key's view on the competition."Legally it is hard to stop players going over and playing in these competitions," Key told the Test Match Special podcast. "It becomes a moral judgement and players have to be prepared to take the right moral stance."Personally, and it is easy for me to say, I would not go and play. But it is down to the player to make that decision."The ECB has refused to schedule bilateral cricket with Afghanistan since the Taliban returned to power in the country in 2021.Last year, ECB chair Richard Thompson described the Taliban's oppression of women and girls as "gender apartheid".England have, however, continued to play against Afghanistan at global events, including World Cups in both limited-overs formats and the Champions Trophy."I don't agree with the way women have been treated in Afghanistan," said Key. "The way things happen out there is not something I agree with so it is not something I would go and do."Pope has been handed a new 12-month England contract despite not playing international cricket since the third Ashes Test in Australia last December.He was recalled to the Test squad for the series against Pakistan in the home summer and has stood in as captain on six occasions, including against India at The Oval in 2025.When asked if he had made his feelings clear to Pope, Key replied: "I had that conversation and Ollie will have to make his decision."Before England's last meeting with Afghanistan, at the 2025 Champions Trophy, Labour MP Tonia Antoniazzi led calls for the fixture to be boycotted.In September, she told BBC Sport: "Why are we here again? Women and girls in Afghanistan are denied the same rights as those in our country, and the women's team lives in exile," she said."Does that not concern the players, especially those with daughters, sisters or mothers?"I hope the International Cricket Council (ICC) refuses to sanction this event. Continuing to allow Afghanistan full member status makes a mockery of its own membership criteria."Former England batter Dawid Malan is entered into the APL draft, alongside the likes of Moeen Ali, James Vince and James Rew – Somerset's Rew made his Test debut in June."As players we take our guidance from the ICC and the boards," Malan told the TMS podcast."As a player it is tough because you have what is morally right and what is by the law. I have a daughter and I want her to play sport and get into sport and enjoy it. I fully understand the argument, but at the end of the day I am a cricketer and need to be able to pay my rent and be able to earn a living while I can."England don't play bilateral series against Afghanistan, but they do play them in World Cups – what's the difference? As players, you sometimes want a board decision to be made that says 'we don't think this is right, we are making a stance against it', then the players will buy into it."I don't think anyone agrees with what is happening in Afghanistan, but once something gets approved you sit there as players and say: 'It's a job, and I have to play and do what I need to do', then you're stuck in a position of what is morally right and what is morally not."On Friday, Dean Ahmad, an agent who represents ex-England all-rounder Moeen, wrote on X: "Morality in sport matters, but so does consistency."The Taliban's treatment of women is indefensible. Yet why are cricketers singled out while governments and corporations maintain ties with states accused of serious human rights abuses. Selective outrage isn't morality."

title: Why Halloween is now bigger than Christmas for some attractions
description: Halloween 'bigger than Christmas', say businessesImage source, CATARINA VIEIRAImage caption, Catarina Vieira spends £150 to £200 on Halloween decorati
body: Halloween 'bigger than Christmas', say businessesImage source, CATARINA VIEIRAImage caption, Catarina Vieira spends £150 to £200 on Halloween decorations and eventsByAna da SilvaWest of EnglandHalloween has become so popular that some attractions now make more money from the spooky season than Christmas, operators say.From pumpkin festivals and haunted mazes to zombie experiences, businesses say demand for Halloween events has soared as the celebration grows from a single night into a month-long attraction.At Avon Valley Adventure Park near Bath, Halloween activities now generate around a third of the site's annual income. Founder Doug Douglas said: "Halloween is really important for us, it has surpassed Christmas.""We make half of our turnover in October, and one third comes from the week of Halloween alone," said David Gaze, owner at Chaplins fancy dress shop in Bristol.Retailers, farm attractions and scare parks say people are spending more on costumes, decorations and immersive experiences, helping to make October one of their busiest times of the year.Chaplins has been a staple in the city centre for 35 years, back when people wore fancy dress on New Year's Eve. "People don't do that so much anymore, now it's mostly for Halloween," Gaze said.Last year, it saw its busiest October to date, with customers individually spending an average of £40 on fancy costumes and accessories."People are spending more and the week of Halloween is our busiest every year, we get queues outside the front door.""It's usually what people are seeing on TV that sells well. Some years ago it was boiler suits from Squid Game, everyone wanted that," he added.Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Guard suits from the Netflix show Squid Game have been a popular Halloween costume since the series came out in 2021Halloween's growing popularity is also benefiting supermarkets and retailers selling sweets, decorations and party supplies.In a survey carried out in March by market researcher IGD, external, 36% of shoppers said they planned to celebrate Halloween this year, up from 27% in 2025. Harvir Dhillon, lead economist at the British Retail Consortium, said at this time of year "retailers will be competing hard" as they see "greater demand for sweets and chocolate, as well as decorations and costumes"."Halloween has become an increasingly popular occasion for people to enjoy," he said.Image source, SOUL MEDIA UKImage caption, Scare attractions like FEAR, near Bath, now run throughout OctoberAnd some like to start celebrations as early as possible, like Catarina Vieira, who lives in Swindon and started decorating her house last week."I spend between £150 to £200 every year on Halloween," she said, adding that is mostly on decorations and thrill events.Vieira said feeling scared about monsters is a "fun escape" from the stresses of her everyday life as an A&E doctor."I think having a holiday where you are scared about something that is 'real', instead of the usual daily mental pressures, touches me in a way.""It helps me escape reality for a bit, being scared about something that is tangibly scary, like monsters or bats," she added.Image source, SOUL MEDIA UKImage caption, Pumpkin patches are "a real festival", says operator Avon Valley Adventure Park But it is not just retail. Many farmers have found ways to diversify their land, by turning it into lucrative family attractions on Halloween.In October, pumpkin patches where you can pick your own pumpkin are high in demand, with popularity being largely driven by social media.Farms often charge an entry fee which can vary significantly, from around £2 to £15 per person, for children and adults alike.With the biggest whoppers selling for upwards of £15 a piece, a fun family day out pushing wheelbarrows full of pumpkins can become costly, yet some attractions sell out quickly.Why are farms embracing Halloween?Heather Parry, managing agent at National Farm Attractions Network (NFAN), said Halloween has become one of the biggest seasons of the year for some farmers."Ten years ago, a pumpkin patch was a field and a wheelbarrow. Now it's a wonderful experience for the whole family," she said.The network has around 200 members and "almost all" embrace the spooky season with a mix of "maize mazes, after-dark trails, scare attractions and pumpkin festivals"."Diversification is key for many farms to thrive," she added, saying it has helped them mitigate existing challenges. Parry said: "Farmers are coping with climate change, change in government support and requirements, high input costs, the changes to inheritance tax relief on farms along with many other things.""Halloween gives farms a short, high-footfall season," she added.'Halloween has surpassed Christmas'Doug Douglas, founder of Avon Valley Adventure Park, said their Halloween events grow every year and now generate a third of their yearly income."We turn over £2m from our activities in October," said Douglas.He added: "Halloween is really important for us, it has surpassed Christmas."The park sits on a 90-acre farm in Keynsham, near Bath, and was once a fruit farm after his dad bought the land more than 30 years ago.Now Douglas runs family activities during school holidays and seasonal events, including for Halloween and Christmas. FEAR Scream Park is their award-winning attraction offering "immersive scare experiences" over 13 nights in October, with scare mazes and live actors.This month, they are expecting around 30,000 visitors but Douglas said the event is not "massively profitable" due to costs."It costs us about £750,000 to put on the event," he said. "On staff wages alone, we employ about 200 staff, including around 120 actors."In addition, they run a popular pumpkin event which attracts around 120,000 people each year.Douglas said: "Everyone thinks they're easy [to put on], but we've got fire shows, stilt walkers, actors, we put in a big bar and we turn it into a real festival field."Image source, Clive BarzilliaImage caption, Clive Barzillia (right) helps run a zombie experience at Gloucester PrisonAt HMP Gloucester, it is zombies that visitors must try and escape from as they walk past old prison cells, facing all sorts of scary encounters.The post-apocalyptic zombie experience 'Salvation-Z' is run by Gloucester Prison Events at the defunct prison and employs around 30 actors from the local area, according to actor manager Clive Barzillia."We get lots and lots of people apply for the acting roles. They have to audition and if they're shy we have to shake it out of them," he said.He said actors are taught welfare training and paramedics are also on site."Ultimately it's a safe environment", he said. "Actors are trained to look out for people that might be vulnerable or sensitive, and they can adapt their acting."He added: "People get right into the spirit of it," talking about the visitors."We've noticed they want to come in fancy dress now, they want to become characters themselves."Follow BBC Bristol on Facebook, external, X, external and Instagram, external. Send your story ideas to us on email or via WhatsApp on 0800 313 4630.Get in touchYour Voice

title: Yorkshire Wildlife Park tiger attack prompts health and safety inquiry
description: Image source, PA MediaImage caption, The park was evacuated after the attack on Saturday afternoonByGrace WoodYorkshireUpdated 5 hours agoA health and
body: Image source, PA MediaImage caption, The park was evacuated after the attack on Saturday afternoonByGrace WoodYorkshireUpdated 5 hours agoA health and safety investigation has been launched into the death of a man who was killed by a tiger after he entered its enclosure.Yorkshire Wildlife Park was closed over the weekend following reports of a man climbing down into the enclosure from a walkway on Saturday afternoon.An eyewitness described seeing the man wearing headphones and "pacing around" near the enclosure before he went in and was attacked. South Yorkshire Police confirmed he was visiting the park on his own."I can confirm that, in line with our statutory duties, the council has launched a health and safety investigation," a City of Doncaster Council spokesperson said.Dan Swaine, the local authority's executive director of place, said the council was "deeply saddened" by the incident and sent its "deepest sympathies" to the man's family and those who were at the scene."We are also working with multiple agencies, including the police and health agencies, and are supporting the Yorkshire Wildlife Park in response to the incident," he said."At this time, we won't be commenting further on the individual or the investigation and we ask that the privacy of those involved is respected at this difficult time."The wildlife park remains closed for third day as investigations continue.A park spokesperson said: "Due to the events over the weekend, the park will remain closed today. Thank you for your understanding."Image source, YappAppImage caption, Police were called to the park at about 13:35 on SaturdaySouth Yorkshire Police said the man died at the scene and his family were being supported by officers. "Our thoughts are with them at this distressing time," the force said.Yorkshire Wildlife Park said the rare Amur tiger, called Altai, remained in the enclosure and would not be euthanised.Cars could be seen coming and going from the park earlier, but there were no visitors.In a message to ticket holders on Monday morning, Yorkshire Wildlife Park said anyone with a booking would be contacted within the next five days to reschedule.Angela Seivewright, 47, from Bawtry, was laying flowers outside the park gates in tribute to the deceased man. She said she had an annual pass and had visited many times with her two children."My daughter was unfortunately sent the video and she's a teenager," she said."I found it very distressing, but I think what I've found more distressing is the reaction of the public that I received when I said I hope the human is OK."I was surprised at the amount of anger and hatred the people seemed to have towards the gentleman."Wildlife park fatal tiger attack - what we know so farOn Saturday evening, police said they were aware of videos circulating online and encouraged people not to share the footage.Image source, Simon Thake/BBCImage caption, Angela Seivewright, who has an annual pass to the park, laid flowers on Monday morningDr Campbell Murn, a previous member of the government's zoo expert committee and lecturer at the University of Reading, said while it was a tragic incident, determined people could get inside zoo enclosures."I view it in the same way a determined thief will get into somebody's house or somebody's car and despite the best security systems and enclosures sometimes these things happen," he said."One of the fundamental approaches of a modern zoo is to give people a wildlife experience and keep them safe so they can learn and they can enjoy being near the animals, but keeping a safety distance that is relevant but not making it too heavy handed."Speaking on BBC Radio 4's Today programme, Murn said public safety was an "enormous consideration" for zoo standards in the UK.A spokesperson for the Born Free Foundation, which campaigns to phase out zoos, called for an "urgent review" into "how the man managed to enter the enclosure and what happened next".Born Free's co-founder Will Travers said: "Putting dangerous wild animals on public display in zoos and safari parks creates a false relationship with humans. "Visitors are encouraged to get up close and personal - that is a deeply unnatural situation and not without risk."Image source, Ella FordImage caption, An eyewitness took this photograph of the tiger minutes before the incidentJo Judge, chief executive of the British and Irish Association of Zoos and Aquariums, said zoos were subject to a "huge number" of risk assessments, along with full inspections every six years and periodic inspections every three.  "There are so many processes and procedures in place to ensure the safety of everybody who is visiting zoos and aquariums and these are incredibly rare incidents," she said."Zoos are actually one of the safest places you can visit."She added the body had received many messages of support for the Yorkshire Wildlife Park."There's no concern from the rest of the community, because we know how well regulated we are, how well licensed we are, all of the procedures and policies that have to be put in place to make sure zoos and aquariums are safe for staff, for the animals and for the public."Image source, Simon Thake/BBCImage caption, The park in South Yorkshire remains closed to visitorsThe tiger has been at Yorkshire Wildlife Park since it was moved from Dyreparken in Norway in February 2025 as part of the international EAZA European Endangered Species Programme for Amur tigers.Dyreparken biologist Helene Axelsen said Altai was born at the site in 2021. She said: "We were deeply saddened to hear about the tragic incident at Yorkshire Wildlife Park over the weekend. "Our thoughts are first and foremost with the victim's family, loved ones, and the entire team at Yorkshire Wildlife Park during this extremely difficult time."Retired animal behaviourist Dr David Sands said anyone entering an enclosure would be seen as a threat."The animal is just being the animal that one million years of evolution has produced," he said. "It's the top apex predator of its group of animals and I don't think any blame can be put on to the animal itself."Could you make the enclosure higher, bigger, more inner protections - well, where do you stop?"Get in touchYour Voice

title: Yorkshire Wildlife Park fatal tiger attack - what we know so far
description: Image source, Ella FordImage caption, Altai the tiger was photographed minutes before the man entered the enclosureByJulia BrysonYorkshire Updated 4 h
body: Image source, Ella FordImage caption, Altai the tiger was photographed minutes before the man entered the enclosureByJulia BrysonYorkshire Updated 4 hours agoYorkshire Wildlife Park near Doncaster remains closed after a man died in the tiger enclosure on Saturday.Here's what we know so far about the attack.What happened at the park?Image source, YappAppImage caption, The park's Land of the Tigers has a raised walkway where visitors can look down on the animalsYorkshire Wildlife Park was busy with visitors when the alarm was raised on Saturday afternoon.Emergency services were called to the park at about 13:30 BST to reports a man had climbed into the tiger enclosure from a high walkway.Visitors were moved away from the area as the tiger attacked the man, who died a short time later.The park confirmed the rare Amur tiger, called Altai, remained safely in the enclosure and would not be euthanised.The park was closed on Saturday and has not yet reopened. How is the park laid out?Image source, YappAppImage caption, The park near Doncaster remained closed for a third day on MondayYorkshire Wildlife Park spans 150 acres with 15 unique habitats featuring wide paths and raised viewing areas.It focuses on large animal conservation, and counts species including lions, meerkats, lemurs, African penguins and sea lions among its residents. The tigers are housed in the park's Land of the Tigers, which has a 300m-long raised walkway so visitors can watch the animals from above.The park's website says people can witness the "majestic cats freely roaming their woodlands and grasslands or playing in their very own waterfall pool".What do we know about the victim?The man has not been named, but eyewitnesses described seeing a man in his 20s on the walkway at the tiger enclosure, wearing headphones and "pacing around" minutes before the incident took place. South Yorkshire Police confirmed he was visiting the park on his own.Speaking to the BBC, Ella Ford, 24, from Wirral, said she saw the same man had climbed up onto the barriers and was spoken to by a woman before "he jumped in and crawled in front of the tiger, where the tiger was perched and just lay there".Ford said she then saw the man shouting for help and the tiger grabbed hold of him. She estimates about 15 to 20 people were on the enclosure's raised visitor walkway before staff quickly evacuated the area, and shortly afterwards, the park.People nearby were confused, she said, and one man was "trying to bang on the fence to try and deter the tiger away, but it obviously wasn't doing anything".What do we know about Altai the tiger?Altai is a rare Amur tiger, also known as a Siberian tiger, the largest big cat in the world.According to the park, the average weight for males is 160-190kg (25-30 stone), while females are smaller, at 110-130kg (17-20 stone).Altai, now five years old, moved to Yorkshire Wildlife Park from Dyreparken in Norway in February 2025. The tiger was moved to Doncaster as part of the international EAZA European Endangered Species Programme for Amur tigers, to join the park's resident tigress Tschuna.Dyreparken biologist Helene Axelsen said: "We were deeply saddened to hear about the tragic incident at Yorkshire Wildlife Park over the weekend."Our thoughts are first and foremost with the victim's family, loved ones, and the entire team at Yorkshire Wildlife Park during this extremely difficult time."What has Yorkshire Wildlife park said?Image source, PA MediaImage caption, Floral tributes have been left at the entrance to the parkA spokesperson for the park thanked everyone who showed concern after the incident.In a statement on Sunday, they said: "Our thoughts and heartfelt sympathies remain with the family and loved ones of the man who tragically lost his life. "The park will be closed today and the staff team who were deeply affected by events will receive specialist support."Many, many people have contacted us about Altai, the tiger. "We can reassure everyone that he is safe and well and will not be euthanised as a result of this incident."Why would a tiger have attacked?Image source, Ella FordImage caption, Tigers are predators which have evolved to attack, said expert Dr David Sands Dr David Sands, a human-companion animal practitioner at the Animal Behavioural Clinic in Chorley, Lancashire, said tigers were predators that would naturally attack. "The animal is just being the animal that a million years of evolution has produced," he said. "It is the top apex predator of its group of animals."I don't think any blame could be put on the animal itself."He added: "Tigers are territorial. This is a male tiger and the incredible weight and power, there's only one outcome because the tiger is in captivity - the enclosure is its territory and a male who can be scented becomes either competition or prey."We're so used to seeing them on the small screen in wildlife documentaries."This is a very big animal that's got the power to bite and break through bones."What happens next?City of Doncaster Council confirmed a health and safety investigation had been launched into the death of the man in the enclosure.Dan Swaine, the local authority's executive director of place, said the council was "deeply saddened" by the incident and sent its "deepest sympathies" to the man's family and those who were at the scene.  "As the relevant licensing authority for the Yorkshire Wildlife Park, I can confirm that, in line with our statutory duties, the council has launched a health and safety investigation," he said. "We are also working with multiple agencies, including the police and health agencies, and are supporting the Yorkshire Wildlife Park in response to the incident."Get in touchYour Voice
